text: Noob question: Can someone please explain the "traces on the card" that reveal it to be an 8X gpu?
author: @optimusminimus-v3d

text:
Very rough and generic answer here: If you look closely at the card's PCIe connector, you'll see that only half of it contains copper connections, while the rest is bare. Those connections correspond to traces on the board (which the arrows point to at 01:32), which transmit signals between the PCIe slot connection and the rest of the card's circuitry. 

Since the card is designed to fit into a PCIe slot with 16 lanes, but only half are being used, it's simple to deduce that it's only using eight PCIe lanes, making it an 8x card.

text:
I know this probably won't be a popular opinion, but from a purely business perspective, I'm honestly surprised that Nvidia is still making anything below the xx80 or xx90-tier GPUs. It just doesn't seem to make much sense on paper. These lower-tier cards, like the xx70 and down, almost feel like an afterthought. It seems like they release them not because they have to, but just because they can or maybe to keep up the appearance of covering the whole market.

Realistically, I wouldn't be surprised if the only reason these cards exist is because of leftover silicon that couldn't meet the specs for higher-tier chips. Classic binning. Might as well use every wafer you can, even the ones that don't quite cut it for the top-end stuff. That makes more sense than Nvidia actively trying to cater to budget gamers out of some kind of goodwill. Let's be real, Nvidia doesn't exactly have a reputation for doing things out of the kindness of their heart.

What’s more interesting is how this could play out going forward. Given the constant push toward higher margins and premium products, I wouldn't be shocked if Nvidia eventually stops making anything below the 80-tier. Or at least stops making anything under $1000.ike, if manufacturing gets so good that barely any silicon goes to waste, it might not even be worth making lower-tier GPUs at all.  With AI, datacenter, and enterprise demand through the roof, the lower-end consumer GPU market might not even be worth their time anymore.

That’s not to say there’s zero value in offering a full product stack. But you have to wonder how long they'll keep doing it if the profit margins aren't there and they can just let AMD or Intel take care of the budget segment. Honestly, the idea of Nvidia pulling back from the mid- and low-tier GPU market doesn't seem far-fetched at all, especially if they can keep dominating the high end and everything related to AI.

text:
I would really like to see GPU frame time as apposed to FPS when testing GPUs, if possible.

To see why this would be better, here's an example:
- CPU takes 15ms to tick a frame (an exagerated CPU bottleneck for demonstration)
- GPU A takes 3ms to render a frame (total 18ms, or 55 FPS)
- GPU B takes 0.5ms to render a frame (total 15.5ms, or 64 FPS)

Using GPU time, you can see that GPU B is 600% faster than GPU A.
But with FPS, which is bottlenecked by the CPU, it only shows a 16.3% improvement.

So when comparing GPUs, I believe this metric is more representative of the GPUs performance.

Going with 3nm would’ve been too expensive, it would’ve made the 5060ti be a 600 USD card.
Worse when you consider games aren’t being optimized as well compared to the 10 series or 20 series era. Like usually the 60 super/ti class cards would be 1080p for intensive games, and 1440p for average modern games, but now you can only really get 1440p 60fps with slightly older games, even to the point where the 5090 isn’t a full 8K card sometimes because of that, despite the 4090 easily handling games at the cards release at 8K.
We’re in a time where the big three have to slow down and develop these cards for longer. Like they should all release cards in every tier, including the 75 watt and lower tier for people stuck on older systems.

@bigturkey1  240hz still isn't 500hz. You understand why a 4k monitor can't do 500hz (at least not yet), right? Usually, when you get a TV, it can't do much past 120hz. Oled looks great (glare does not, hope you have it in a windowless basement), but then burn in still exists and OLED isn't quite where it needs to be yet. 

Monitors, on the other hand, tend to feature either high resolution, or high refresh rate. More expensive monitors will tend to offer a choice between both: a 'cinematic' mode for 4k movie watching at lower refresh rate (60hz or whatever the video is shot at), or a gaming mode at 1080p with super high refresh rate, something like 380 or 480 or 540 and then you get extra frame information in games that can actually push those frames (CS:Go is a common one). 

Imagine seeing someone a full 240 frames faster than they can see you, in a game where headshots through doorways and around corners, matters. 

I'm not saying there's anything bad about 4k, or gaming at lower refresh rates. I am saying there are a ton of sacrifices involved and there's a reason why people who are trying to get the most performance out of a gaming scenario, competitively, end up doing things such as turning resolution to 1080, turning down settings, and then turning up refresh rate as high as it can be (on a supported panel). 

Factually, there just isn't a 500hz option for something at 4k resolution, and there isn't a GPU capable of pushing it, should a panel exist. At least, not yet.

If they architecture cards for 24gb ram - and it's easy to halve that to create a 12gb card at a lower price point - and then maybe halve again so you have 24gb/12gb and 6gb cards.

Similarly if you create a 16gb design that you halve to 8gb. But if you wanted an 8gb and a 12gb, otherwise the same, you need 2 different designs and its not cost effective to do that. Your 8gb card would end up being more or less the same price as 12gb. That's why at the top end you had 24gb and 12gb and mid / lower end you have 16/8. That said, now they've started putting 32gb in the top end then the 32/16/8 thing should work again and you'll see 16gb where there was 12gb. Maybe this gen they'll do a super version like that or maybe it'll be next series.

From a player perspective though it rarely made sense to buy the 16gb version of these because they lack performance and few games took any advantage of the extra vram. It was like an option to sell what looks like a bigger spec and get an extra £100 from fools. Now though, perhaps more games are over the 8gb. Thing is, if they go over 8gb, it's unlikely they are hitting 16gb, because it's not like when GPUs had megabytes of ram and doubling 4mb to 8mb it was easy to fill that 4mb. That said there is more than just textures using up vram these days - but these midrange cards tend to be slow with the features anyway so you'd probably be better with a 5070 if you want to use those even with less vram. And if you really think you need 16gb then the 5070ti is the card - but that's not cheap. Bottom line : a lot of people with older gen mid range cards that had 16gb just wasted their money - the cheaper 8gb was the thing to get. Today, it depends what games you want to play but 12gb is probably enough and the reason for the 16gb is really to do with the board design and how you can halve the memory by not putting ram chips in a few of the PCBs, but would have to do more work to have 8gb and 12gb versions.
